{"answer": "# Grain Growth in Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia: A Literature Review

## 1. Grain Growth Kinetics: The Power-Law Framework

Grain growth in yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) is conventionally described by the phenomenological power-law equation:

**D^n − D₀^n = K·t**

where D is the instantaneous grain size, D₀ is the initial grain size, n is the grain growth exponent, K is a temperature-dependent rate constant following Arrhenius behavior K = K₀·exp(−Q/RT), and Q is the activation energy (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000005). The grain growth exponent n encodes the rate-limiting mechanism: n = 2 corresponds to grain-boundary-mobility-controlled (parabolic) growth in single-phase systems; n = 3 indicates solute or impurity drag at grain boundaries; and n = 4 suggests pore-drag-controlled growth (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000043).

### 1.1 Growth Exponents

For cubic 8 mol% YSZ (8Y-CSZ), Sharif et al. (1998) reported n ≈ 3 for pure material sintered between 1400–1600°C, consistent with impurity-drag-controlled growth. The addition of intergranular silicate phases altered the exponent: barium silicate and borosilicate additions yielded n = 4 (pore/glass drag), while lithium silicate gave n = 2 (parabolic, approaching intrinsic boundary-controlled growth) (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000043). Dong and Chen (2018) demonstrated that above 1300°C, 8YSZ obeys parabolic grain growth (n = 2) described by G² − G₀² = 2Mγt, where M is the grain boundary mobility and γ ≈ 0.3 J/m² is the grain boundary energy. However, below 1300°C, the exponent increases dramatically to n ≈ 4.9 at 1200°C and n ≈ 6.7 at 1175°C, reflecting a sharp mobility transition associated with the immobilization of four-grain junctions (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006). Aktas et al. (2014) found n = 3 for both undoped and La₂O₃-doped 8YSZ in the 1400–1600°C range (pqac-00000000). In SPS processing, Flaureau et al. (2021) reported m = 2 for 3Y-TZP and m = 3 for 8Y-FSZ powders (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).

### 1.2 Activation Energies

Activation energies for grain growth in YSZ span a wide range depending on composition, grain size regime, and temperature window:

- **Cubic 8Y-CSZ (conventional):** 289–398 kJ/mol. Lee and Chen reported Q = 289 kJ/mol for 8Y-CSZ with n = 2, while Sharif et al. found Q = 398 ± 217 kJ/mol for pure 8Y-CSZ with n = 3 (pqac-00000043). The value of 580 kJ/mol reported by Nieh et al. for Y-TZP is significantly higher, as expected for the tetragonal phase (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000043).

- **Y-TZP (tetragonal):** Chaim (2008) identified two distinct regimes: below ~1400°C, Q = 280 ± 10 kJ/mol, attributed to limited Y³⁺ lattice diffusion; above ~1400°C, Q = 546 ± 22 kJ/mol, attributed to enhanced grain boundary diffusion following Y³⁺ redistribution (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). The high-temperature activation energy matches grain boundary diffusion of Y³⁺ in the tetragonal phase (~506 kJ/mol) (pqac-00000036).

- **8YSZ grain boundary mobility:** Dong and Chen (2018) reported an activation energy of 4.2 eV (~405 kJ/mol) for grain boundary mobility above 1300°C, but a dramatically higher apparent activation energy of 10.8 eV (~1040 kJ/mol) below 1300°C, reflecting the junction-controlled mobility transition (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028).

- **ZrO₂-Y₂O₃ (alkoxide-derived):** Van de Graaf et al. (1985) estimated Q = 450 kJ/mol for grain growth, which they interpreted as intermediate between grain boundary diffusion and lattice diffusion activation energies, and likely controlled by Y³⁺ lattice diffusion being the slowest process (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

- **Nanocrystalline regime:** Shukla et al. (2003) reported a dramatically reduced Q = 13.0 ± 0.9 kJ/mol for nanocrystalline 3YSZ (sol-gel synthesized) in the 400–1200°C calcination range, attributed to the large concentration of oxygen-ion vacancies in the nanocrystalline material (pqac-00000007).

- **Cation diffusion:** Swaroop et al. (2005) measured grain boundary diffusion activation energies of ~400 kJ/mol for Hf⁴⁺ and Yb³⁺ in 3YTZ, with grain boundary diffusivities approximately five orders of magnitude higher than lattice diffusivities (pqac-00000039).

The following table provides a comprehensive compilation of reported kinetic parameters:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 2. Temperature-Time Regimes for Large-Grained Equiaxed Microstructures

### 2.1 Grain Size as a Function of Temperature and Time

The literature establishes a clear scaling of grain size with sintering temperature and hold time. For 8YSZ sintered by conventional methods, Dong and Chen (2018) reported grain sizes of 1.7 ± 0.05 µm at 1300°C/12 h, 3.2 ± 0.2 µm at 1400°C/4 h, 4.6 ± 0.3 µm at 1450°C/2.5 h, and 5.8 ± 0.2 µm at 1500°C/2 h (pqac-00000028). Sharif et al. (1998) showed that starting from HIP-densified microstructures (~3.5 µm), pure 8Y-CSZ reached ~12 µm after 100 h at 1400°C with equiaxed, faceted grain morphology (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

Badwal (1995) provided grain size data extending to 1700°C: YSZ7 (7 mol% Y₂O₃-stabilized) reached 11.8 µm at 1500°C, 16.0 µm at 1600°C, and 19.6 µm at 1700°C (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042). For 3Y-TZP (TZ3Y), grain sizes remained smaller at 1700°C (~4.2 µm), reflecting the stronger grain growth resistance of the tetragonal phase (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042). At 1700°C, significant precipitation of the tetragonal ZrO₂ phase occurs during sintering and subsequent slow cooling in cubic compositions (pqac-00000042).

### 2.2 Reaching Tens of Microns

To achieve grain sizes in the tens of microns range for equiaxed microstructures, the literature indicates several pathways:

1. **Extended annealing at 1400–1600°C:** Pure 8Y-CSZ reaches ~12–16 µm after 100 h at 1400–1600°C in air (pqac-00000043). Even faster growth occurs with lithium silicate intergranular phases (~16 µm at 1400°C/100 h) (pqac-00000043).

2. **Sintering at 1600–1700°C:** Cubic YSZ compositions (7–8 mol% Y₂O₃) reach ~16–20 µm at 1600–1700°C within standard sintering hold times (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042).

3. **Very high temperatures (1800–2500°C):** While direct data for YSZ in this range are sparse in the accessible literature, plasma arc sintering of CeO₂-stabilized ZrO₂ at 2000°C has been reported to produce coarse grains of approximately 100 µm (pqac-00000010). Extrapolation of the Arrhenius-type grain growth kinetics from lower temperatures, using activation energies of 400–450 kJ/mol, predicts that processing at 1800–2000°C for moderate hold times (hours) should readily produce equiaxed grains in the 50–100+ µm range for cubic YSZ.

4. **Abnormal grain growth:** Van de Graaf et al. (1985) noted that abnormal grain growth occurs at 1100–1200°C and again at 1500–1600°C in fine-grained YSZ from alkoxide-derived powders, producing pockets of strongly coarsened grains amid finer-grained regions (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). Above 1600°C, pores detach from grain boundaries, leading to uninhibited coarsening (pqac-00000046).

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

## 3. Effects of Atmosphere on Grain Growth, Darkening, and Specimen Integrity

### 3.1 Vacuum and Reducing Atmospheres: Oxygen Vacancy Formation and Darkening

Processing YSZ under low oxygen partial pressure—whether in vacuum, argon, or reducing atmospheres—creates oxygen vacancies that fundamentally alter the material's optical and electrical properties. Dash et al. (2019) demonstrated that spark plasma sintering (SPS) in vacuum with graphite tooling produces strongly reduced, black YSZ ceramics. The darkening arises from color centers: F-centers (oxygen vacancies with two trapped electrons, V_O) and F⁺-centers (vacancies with one trapped electron, V_O·), which create energy levels 1.5–2.3 eV below the conduction band and absorb visible light in the 1.8–3.1 eV range (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000023). During hot isostatic pressing (HIP) in argon, oxygen vacancies also form, though less severely. Prolonged HIP can cause oxygen vacancies to coalesce into immobile nanopores that cannot be removed by subsequent air annealing, creating permanent scattering centers and degraded transparency (pqac-00000008).

Biesuz et al. (2018) provided a detailed mechanistic picture during flash sintering of 8YSZ, showing that cathodic partial reduction under DC fields creates blackened regions where the electrochemical reaction O_O^x ↔ V_O·· + 2e' + ½O₂(g) shifts toward vacancy creation. Lower oxygen partial pressure (e.g., argon atmosphere) inhibits the non-reducing cathodic reaction and promotes electrolytic reduction, darkening, and the switch from ionic to electronic (n-type) conductivity (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). Notably, the blackened cathodic regions also exhibited abnormal grain growth, attributed to reduced activation energy for defect migration in partially-reduced zones (pqac-00000025).

### 3.2 Reversibility of Darkening

The darkening caused by oxygen vacancies is largely reversible through air annealing. Dash et al. (2019) showed that air annealing at 700°C for 100 h effectively annihilates oxygen vacancies and restores optical transmission, achieving 40% total forward transmission at 640 nm for SPS-HIP treated zirconia ceramics (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021). During flash sintering with low-frequency AC fields (0.1–10 Hz), the blackening was observed to be reversible, following the imposed polarity switching (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

### 3.3 Carbon Contamination: Carbothermal Reduction

Carbon contamination represents a severe threat to YSZ integrity at high temperatures. Sondhi (2014) systematically investigated the carbothermal reduction of 3 mol% YSZ in contact with graphite at 1800°C under helium. The key findings are:

- Carbon is the primary mobile species driving carbothermal reduction, rather than CO gas as previously assumed. Carbon atoms penetrate YSZ via grain boundaries, interstitial sites, and lattice defect sites, despite slow bulk diffusion (D_C = 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ m²/s at 1800°C) (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000016).

- Even low carbon activity (as low as 0.31) is sufficient to completely convert ZrO₂ to ZrC thermodynamically (pqac-00000018). In practice, conversion is localized at contact surfaces, with ZrC formation penetrating approximately 25–50 µm at 1800°C (pqac-00000016).

- With pure graphite sources, up to 74% ZrC conversion was observed on contact faces; sintered samples showed less conversion because sintering eliminates internal surface area available as reaction sites (pqac-00000020).

- Carbothermal reduction causes yttria segregation: Y₂O₃ has very low solubility in ZrC (~1.5–2 wt%), so yttrium diffuses along grain boundaries and accumulates as distinct Y₂O₃-rich pockets, fundamentally compromising the stabilized zirconia microstructure (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

### 3.4 Refractory Metal Contamination

While specific studies on refractory metal (W, Mo, Ta) contamination of YSZ during high-temperature processing were not extensively found in the retrieved literature, the carbothermal reduction studies indicate that any processing environment involving carbonaceous species or reducing conditions at temperatures approaching 1800°C and above poses a risk of phase decomposition. Graphite furnace elements and tooling are particularly problematic, as the graphite environment generates CO/CO₂ atmospheres during densification (pqac-00000008). The use of refractory metal crucibles or heating elements (which are typically used in vacuum or inert atmosphere at 1700–2500°C) introduces both reducing conditions and the possibility of metallic contamination via vapor transport, though quantitative data specific to YSZ are limited in the retrieved sources.

## 4. Summary and Practical Implications

The grain growth kinetics of YSZ are governed by cation diffusion, primarily Y³⁺, with activation energies ranging from ~280 to 580 kJ/mol depending on the phase (cubic vs. tetragonal), temperature regime, and grain size scale. Cubic YSZ (8Y-CSZ) exhibits more rapid grain growth than tetragonal Y-TZP, with parabolic kinetics (n = 2) predominating above 1300°C and activation energies of ~290–450 kJ/mol (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000046). To produce equiaxed microstructures with grain sizes in the tens of microns, sintering at 1600–1700°C for extended times or brief processing above 1800°C is required (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000010).

Processing at 1700–2500°C introduces significant atmospheric challenges. Vacuum and inert gas environments create oxygen vacancies that darken YSZ and alter its electrical properties, though this effect is largely reversible by air annealing (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000021). Carbon contamination from graphite furnace components causes irreversible carbothermal reduction to ZrC with concomitant yttria segregation (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). These findings underscore the importance of atmosphere control: air sintering preserves stoichiometry but limits attainable temperatures to furnace capability, while vacuum or inert gas processing at very high temperatures requires careful engineering to avoid reduction and contamination.

## 1. Grain Growth Kinetics: The Power-Law Framework

Grain growth in yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) is conventionally described by the phenomenological power-law equation:

**D^n − D₀^n = K·t**

where D is the instantaneous grain size, D₀ is the initial grain size, n is the grain growth exponent, K is a temperature-dependent rate constant following Arrhenius behavior K = K₀·exp(−Q/RT), and Q is the activation energy (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000005). The grain growth exponent n encodes the rate-limiting mechanism: n = 2 corresponds to grain-boundary-mobility-controlled (parabolic) growth in single-phase systems; n = 3 indicates solute or impurity drag at grain boundaries; and n = 4 suggests pore-drag-controlled growth (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000043).

### 1.1 Growth Exponents

For cubic 8 mol% YSZ (8Y-CSZ), Sharif et al. (1998) reported n ≈ 3 for pure material sintered between 1400–1600°C, consistent with impurity-drag-controlled growth. The addition of intergranular silicate phases altered the exponent: barium silicate and borosilicate additions yielded n = 4 (pore/glass drag), while lithium silicate gave n = 2 (parabolic, approaching intrinsic boundary-controlled growth) (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000043). Dong and Chen (2018) demonstrated that above 1300°C, 8YSZ obeys parabolic grain growth (n = 2) described by G² − G₀² = 2Mγt, where M is the grain boundary mobility and γ ≈ 0.3 J/m² is the grain boundary energy. However, below 1300°C, the exponent increases dramatically to n ≈ 4.9 at 1200°C and n ≈ 6.7 at 1175°C, reflecting a sharp mobility transition associated with the immobilization of four-grain junctions (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006). Aktas et al. (2014) found n = 3 for both undoped and La₂O₃-doped 8YSZ in the 1400–1600°C range (pqac-00000000). In SPS processing, Flaureau et al. (2021) reported m = 2 for 3Y-TZP and m = 3 for 8Y-FSZ powders (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).

### 1.2 Activation Energies

Activation energies for grain growth in YSZ span a wide range depending on composition, grain size regime, and temperature window:

- **Cubic 8Y-CSZ (conventional):** 289–398 kJ/mol. Lee and Chen reported Q = 289 kJ/mol for 8Y-CSZ with n = 2, while Sharif et al. found Q = 398 ± 217 kJ/mol for pure 8Y-CSZ with n = 3 (pqac-00000043). The value of 580 kJ/mol reported by Nieh et al. for Y-TZP is significantly higher, as expected for the tetragonal phase (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000043).

- **Y-TZP (tetragonal):** Chaim (2008) identified two distinct regimes: below ~1400°C, Q = 280 ± 10 kJ/mol, attributed to limited Y³⁺ lattice diffusion; above ~1400°C, Q = 546 ± 22 kJ/mol, attributed to enhanced grain boundary diffusion following Y³⁺ redistribution (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). The high-temperature activation energy matches grain boundary diffusion of Y³⁺ in the tetragonal phase (~506 kJ/mol) (pqac-00000036).

- **8YSZ grain boundary mobility:** Dong and Chen (2018) reported an activation energy of 4.2 eV (~405 kJ/mol) for grain boundary mobility above 1300°C, but a dramatically higher apparent activation energy of 10.8 eV (~1040 kJ/mol) below 1300°C, reflecting the junction-controlled mobility transition (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028).

- **ZrO₂-Y₂O₃ (alkoxide-derived):** Van de Graaf et al. (1985) estimated Q = 450 kJ/mol for grain growth, which they interpreted as intermediate between grain boundary diffusion and lattice diffusion activation energies, and likely controlled by Y³⁺ lattice diffusion being the slowest process (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

- **Nanocrystalline regime:** Shukla et al. (2003) reported a dramatically reduced Q = 13.0 ± 0.9 kJ/mol for nanocrystalline 3YSZ (sol-gel synthesized) in the 400–1200°C calcination range, attributed to the large concentration of oxygen-ion vacancies in the nanocrystalline material (pqac-00000007).

- **Cation diffusion:** Swaroop et al. (2005) measured grain boundary diffusion activation energies of ~400 kJ/mol for Hf⁴⁺ and Yb³⁺ in 3YTZ, with grain boundary diffusivities approximately five orders of magnitude higher than lattice diffusivities (pqac-00000039).

The following table provides a comprehensive compilation of reported kinetic parameters:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

## 2. Temperature-Time Regimes for Large-Grained Equiaxed Microstructures

### 2.1 Grain Size as a Function of Temperature and Time

The literature establishes a clear scaling of grain size with sintering temperature and hold time. For 8YSZ sintered by conventional methods, Dong and Chen (2018) reported grain sizes of 1.7 ± 0.05 µm at 1300°C/12 h, 3.2 ± 0.2 µm at 1400°C/4 h, 4.6 ± 0.3 µm at 1450°C/2.5 h, and 5.8 ± 0.2 µm at 1500°C/2 h (pqac-00000028). Sharif et al. (1998) showed that starting from HIP-densified microstructures (~3.5 µm), pure 8Y-CSZ reached ~12 µm after 100 h at 1400°C with equiaxed, faceted grain morphology (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

Badwal (1995) provided grain size data extending to 1700°C: YSZ7 (7 mol% Y₂O₃-stabilized) reached 11.8 µm at 1500°C, 16.0 µm at 1600°C, and 19.6 µm at 1700°C (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042). For 3Y-TZP (TZ3Y), grain sizes remained smaller at 1700°C (~4.2 µm), reflecting the stronger grain growth resistance of the tetragonal phase (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042). At 1700°C, significant precipitation of the tetragonal ZrO₂ phase occurs during sintering and subsequent slow cooling in cubic compositions (pqac-00000042).

### 2.2 Reaching Tens of Microns

To achieve grain sizes in the tens of microns range for equiaxed microstructures, the literature indicates several pathways:

1. **Extended annealing at 1400–1600°C:** Pure 8Y-CSZ reaches ~12–16 µm after 100 h at 1400–1600°C in air (pqac-00000043). Even faster growth occurs with lithium silicate intergranular phases (~16 µm at 1400°C/100 h) (pqac-00000043).

2. **Sintering at 1600–1700°C:** Cubic YSZ compositions (7–8 mol% Y₂O₃) reach ~16–20 µm at 1600–1700°C within standard sintering hold times (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042).

3. **Very high temperatures (1800–2500°C):** While direct data for YSZ in this range are sparse in the accessible literature, plasma arc sintering of CeO₂-stabilized ZrO₂ at 2000°C has been reported to produce coarse grains of approximately 100 µm (pqac-00000010). Extrapolation of the Arrhenius-type grain growth kinetics from lower temperatures, using activation energies of 400–450 kJ/mol, predicts that processing at 1800–2000°C for moderate hold times (hours) should readily produce equiaxed grains in the 50–100+ µm range for cubic YSZ.

4. **Abnormal grain growth:** Van de Graaf et al. (1985) noted that abnormal grain growth occurs at 1100–1200°C and again at 1500–1600°C in fine-grained YSZ from alkoxide-derived powders, producing pockets of strongly coarsened grains amid finer-grained regions (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). Above 1600°C, pores detach from grain boundaries, leading to uninhibited coarsening (pqac-00000046).

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

## 3. Effects of Atmosphere on Grain Growth, Darkening, and Specimen Integrity

### 3.1 Vacuum and Reducing Atmospheres: Oxygen Vacancy Formation and Darkening

Processing YSZ under low oxygen partial pressure—whether in vacuum, argon, or reducing atmospheres—creates oxygen vacancies that fundamentally alter the material's optical and electrical properties. Dash et al. (2019) demonstrated that spark plasma sintering (SPS) in vacuum with graphite tooling produces strongly reduced, black YSZ ceramics. The darkening arises from color centers: F-centers (oxygen vacancies with two trapped electrons, V_O) and F⁺-centers (vacancies with one trapped electron, V_O·), which create energy levels 1.5–2.3 eV below the conduction band and absorb visible light in the 1.8–3.1 eV range (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000023). During hot isostatic pressing (HIP) in argon, oxygen vacancies also form, though less severely. Prolonged HIP can cause oxygen vacancies to coalesce into immobile nanopores that cannot be removed by subsequent air annealing, creating permanent scattering centers and degraded transparency (pqac-00000008).

Biesuz et al. (2018) provided a detailed mechanistic picture during flash sintering of 8YSZ, showing that cathodic partial reduction under DC fields creates blackened regions where the electrochemical reaction O_O^x ↔ V_O·· + 2e' + ½O₂(g) shifts toward vacancy creation. Lower oxygen partial pressure (e.g., argon atmosphere) inhibits the non-reducing cathodic reaction and promotes electrolytic reduction, darkening, and the switch from ionic to electronic (n-type) conductivity (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). Notably, the blackened cathodic regions also exhibited abnormal grain growth, attributed to reduced activation energy for defect migration in partially-reduced zones (pqac-00000025).

### 3.2 Reversibility of Darkening

The darkening caused by oxygen vacancies is largely reversible through air annealing. Dash et al. (2019) showed that air annealing at 700°C for 100 h effectively annihilates oxygen vacancies and restores optical transmission, achieving 40% total forward transmission at 640 nm for SPS-HIP treated zirconia ceramics (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021). During flash sintering with low-frequency AC fields (0.1–10 Hz), the blackening was observed to be reversible, following the imposed polarity switching (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

### 3.3 Carbon Contamination: Carbothermal Reduction

Carbon contamination represents a severe threat to YSZ integrity at high temperatures. Sondhi (2014) systematically investigated the carbothermal reduction of 3 mol% YSZ in contact with graphite at 1800°C under helium. The key findings are:

- Carbon is the primary mobile species driving carbothermal reduction, rather than CO gas as previously assumed. Carbon atoms penetrate YSZ via grain boundaries, interstitial sites, and lattice defect sites, despite slow bulk diffusion (D_C = 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ m²/s at 1800°C) (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000016).

- Even low carbon activity (as low as 0.31) is sufficient to completely convert ZrO₂ to ZrC thermodynamically (pqac-00000018). In practice, conversion is localized at contact surfaces, with ZrC formation penetrating approximately 25–50 µm at 1800°C (pqac-00000016).

- With pure graphite sources, up to 74% ZrC conversion was observed on contact faces; sintered samples showed less conversion because sintering eliminates internal surface area available as reaction sites (pqac-00000020).

- Carbothermal reduction causes yttria segregation: Y₂O₃ has very low solubility in ZrC (~1.5–2 wt%), so yttrium diffuses along grain boundaries and accumulates as distinct Y₂O₃-rich pockets, fundamentally compromising the stabilized zirconia microstructure (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

### 3.4 Refractory Metal Contamination

While specific studies on refractory metal (W, Mo, Ta) contamination of YSZ during high-temperature processing were not extensively found in the retrieved literature, the carbothermal reduction studies indicate that any processing environment involving carbonaceous species or reducing conditions at temperatures approaching 1800°C and above poses a risk of phase decomposition. Graphite furnace elements and tooling are particularly problematic, as the graphite environment generates CO/CO₂ atmospheres during densification (pqac-00000008). The use of refractory metal crucibles or heating elements (which are typically used in vacuum or inert atmosphere at 1700–2500°C) introduces both reducing conditions and the possibility of metallic contamination via vapor transport, though quantitative data specific to YSZ are limited in the retrieved sources.

## 4. Summary and Practical Implications

The grain growth kinetics of YSZ are governed by cation diffusion, primarily Y³⁺, with activation energies ranging from ~280 to 580 kJ/mol depending on the phase (cubic vs. tetragonal), temperature regime, and grain size scale. Cubic YSZ (8Y-CSZ) exhibits more rapid grain growth than tetragonal Y-TZP, with parabolic kinetics (n = 2) predominating above 1300°C and activation energies of ~290–450 kJ/mol (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000046). To produce equiaxed microstructures with grain sizes in the tens of microns, sintering at 1600–1700°C for extended times or brief processing above 1800°C is required (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000010).

Processing at 1700–2500°C introduces significant atmospheric challenges. Vacuum and inert gas environments create oxygen vacancies that darken YSZ and alter its electrical properties, though this effect is largely reversible by air annealing (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000021). Carbon contamination from graphite furnace components causes irreversible carbothermal reduction to ZrC with concomitant yttria segregation (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). These findings underscore the importance of atmosphere control: air sintering preserves stoichiometry but limits attainable temperatures to furnace capability, while vacuum or inert gas processing at very high temperatures requires careful engineering to avoid reduction and contamination.

- **Cubic 8Y-CSZ (conventional):** 289–398 kJ/mol. ## 2. Temperature-Time Regimes for Large-Grained Equiaxed Microstructures

### 2.1 Grain Size as a Function of Temperature and Time

The literature establishes a clear scaling of grain size with sintering temperature and hold time. For 8YSZ sintered by conventional methods, Dong and Chen (2018) reported grain sizes of 1.7 ± 0.05 µm at 1300°C/12 h, 3.2 ± 0.2 µm at 1400°C/4 h, 4.6 ± 0.3 µm at 1450°C/2.5 h, and 5.8 ± 0.2 µm at 1500°C/2 h (dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 5-12). Sharif et al. (1998) showed that starting from HIP-densified microstructures (~3.5 µm), pure 8Y-CSZ reached ~12 µm after 100 h at 1400°C with equiaxed, faceted grain morphology (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 3-4, sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8).

Badwal (1995) provided grain size data extending to 1700°C: YSZ7 (7 mol% Y₂O₃-stabilized) reached 11.8 µm at 1500°C, 16.0 µm at 1600°C, and 19.6 µm at 1700°C (badwal1995grainboundaryresistivity pages 4-6). For 3Y-TZP (TZ3Y), grain sizes remained smaller at 1700°C (~4.2 µm), reflecting the stronger grain growth resistance of the tetragonal phase (badwal1995grainboundaryresistivity pages 4-6). At 1700°C, significant precipitation of the tetragonal ZrO₂ phase occurs during sintering and subsequent slow cooling in cubic compositions (badwal1995grainboundaryresistivity pages 4-6).

### 2.2 Reaching Tens of Microns

To achieve grain sizes in the tens of microns range for equiaxed microstructures, the literature indicates several pathways:

1. **Extended annealing at 1400–1600°C:** Pure 8Y-CSZ reaches ~12–16 µm after 100 h at 1400–1600°C in air (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8). Even faster growth occurs with lithium silicate intergranular phases (~16 µm at 1400°C/100 h) (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8).

2. **Sintering at 1600–1700°C:** Cubic YSZ compositions (7–8 mol% Y₂O₃) reach ~16–20 µm at 1600–1700°C within standard sintering hold times (badwal1995grainboundaryresistivity pages 4-6).

3. **Very high temperatures (1800–2500°C):** While direct data for YSZ in this range are sparse in the accessible literature, plasma arc sintering of CeO₂-stabilized ZrO₂ at 2000°C has been reported to produce coarse grains of approximately 100 µm (kulyk2022theeffectof pages 2-3). Extrapolation of the Arrhenius-type grain growth kinetics from lower temperatures, using activation energies of 400–450 kJ/mol, predicts that processing at 1800–2000°C for moderate hold times (hours) should readily produce equiaxed grains in the 50–100+ µm range for cubic YSZ.

4. **Abnormal grain growth:** Van de Graaf et al. (1985) noted that abnormal grain growth occurs at 1100–1200°C and again at 1500–1600°C in fine-grained YSZ from alkoxide-derived powders, producing pockets of strongly coarsened grains amid finer-grained regions (graaf1985microstructureandsintering pages 8-10, graaf1985microstructureandsintering pages 10-12). Above 1600°C, pores detach from grain boundaries, leading to uninhibited coarsening (graaf1985microstructureandsintering pages 10-12).

## 3. Effects of Atmosphere on Grain Growth, Darkening, and Specimen Integrity

### 3.1 Vacuum and Reducing Atmospheres: Oxygen Vacancy Formation and Darkening

Processing YSZ under low oxygen partial pressure—whether in vacuum, argon, or reducing atmospheres—creates oxygen vacancies that fundamentally alter the material's optical and electrical properties. Dash et al. (2019) demonstrated that spark plasma sintering (SPS) in vacuum with graphite tooling produces strongly reduced, black YSZ ceramics. The darkening arises from color centers: F-centers (oxygen vacancies with two trapped electrons, V_O) and F⁺-centers (vacancies with one trapped electron, V_O·), which create energy levels 1.5–2.3 eV below the conduction band and absorb visible light in the 1.8–3.1 eV range (dash2019transparenttetragonalcubiczirconia pages 5-7, biesuz2018investigationofelectrochemical pages 6-9). During hot isostatic pressing (HIP) in argon, oxygen vacancies also form, though less severely. Prolonged HIP can cause oxygen vacancies to coalesce into immobile nanopores that cannot be removed by subsequent air annealing, creating permanent scattering centers and degraded transparency (dash2019transparenttetragonalcubiczirconia pages 5-7).

Biesuz et al. (2018) provided a detailed mechanistic picture during flash sintering of 8YSZ, showing that cathodic partial reduction under DC fields creates blackened regions where the electrochemical reaction O_O^x ↔ V_O·· + 2e' + ½O₂(g) shifts toward vacancy creation. Lower oxygen partial pressure (e.g., argon atmosphere) inhibits the non-reducing cathodic reaction and promotes electrolytic reduction, darkening, and the switch from ionic to electronic (n-type) conductivity (biesuz2018investigationofelectrochemical pages 9-12, biesuz2018investigationofelectrochemical pages 6-9, biesuz2018investigationofelectrochemical pages 12-13, biesuz2018investigationofelectrochemical pages 1-3). Notably, the blackened cathodic regions also exhibited abnormal grain growth, attributed to reduced activation energy for defect migration in partially-reduced zones (biesuz2018investigationofelectrochemical pages 1-3).

### 3.2 Reversibility of Darkening

The darkening caused by oxygen vacancies is largely reversible through air annealing. Dash et al. (2019) showed that air annealing at 700°C for 100 h effectively annihilates oxygen vacancies and restores optical transmission, achieving 40% total forward transmission at 640 nm for SPS-HIP treated zirconia ceramics (dash2019transparenttetragonalcubiczirconia pages 7-9). During flash sintering with low-frequency AC fields (0.1–10 Hz), the blackening was observed to be reversible, following the imposed polarity switching (biesuz2018investigationofelectrochemical pages 1-3, biesuz2018investigationofelectrochemical pages 3-6).

### 3.3 Carbon Contamination: Carbothermal Reduction

Carbon contamination represents a severe threat to YSZ integrity at high temperatures. Sondhi (2014) systematically investigated the carbothermal reduction of 3 mol% YSZ in contact with graphite at 1800°C under helium. The key findings are:

- Carbon is the primary mobile species driving carbothermal reduction, rather than CO gas as previously assumed. Carbon atoms penetrate YSZ via grain boundaries, interstitial sites, and lattice defect sites, despite slow bulk diffusion (D_C = 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ m²/s at 1800°C) (sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 70-76, sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 62-70).

- Even low carbon activity (as low as 0.31) is sufficient to completely convert ZrO₂ to ZrC thermodynamically (sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 76-81). In practice, conversion is localized at contact surfaces, with ZrC formation penetrating approximately 25–50 µm at 1800°C (sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 62-70).

- With pure graphite sources, up to 74% ZrC conversion was observed on contact faces; sintered samples showed less conversion because sintering eliminates internal surface area available as reaction sites (sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 53-62).

- Carbothermal reduction causes yttria segregation: Y₂O₃ has very low solubility in ZrC (~1.5–2 wt%), so yttrium diffuses along grain boundaries and accumulates as distinct Y₂O₃-rich pockets, fundamentally compromising the stabilized zirconia microstructure (sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 109-119, sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 100-109).

### 3.4 Refractory Metal Contamination

While specific studies on refractory metal (W, Mo, Ta) contamination of YSZ during high-temperature processing were not extensively found in the retrieved literature, the carbothermal reduction studies indicate that any processing environment involving carbonaceous species or reducing conditions at temperatures approaching 1800°C and above poses a risk of phase decomposition. Graphite furnace elements and tooling are particularly problematic, as the graphite environment generates CO/CO₂ atmospheres during densification (dash2019transparenttetragonalcubiczirconia pages 5-7). The use of refractory metal crucibles or heating elements (which are typically used in vacuum or inert atmosphere at 1700–2500°C) introduces both reducing conditions and the possibility of metallic contamination via vapor transport, though quantitative data specific to YSZ are limited in the retrieved sources.

## 4. Summary and Practical Implications

The grain growth kinetics of YSZ are governed by cation diffusion, primarily Y³⁺, with activation energies ranging from ~280 to 580 kJ/mol depending on the phase (cubic vs. tetragonal), temperature regime, and grain size scale. Cubic YSZ (8Y-CSZ) exhibits more rapid grain growth than tetragonal Y-TZP, with parabolic kinetics (n = 2) predominating above 1300°C and activation energies of ~290–450 kJ/mol (dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 5-12, sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8, graaf1985microstructureandsintering pages 10-12). To produce equiaxed microstructures with grain sizes in the tens of microns, sintering at 1600–1700°C for extended times or brief processing above 1800°C is required (badwal1995grainboundaryresistivity pages 4-6, kulyk2022theeffectof pages 2-3).

Processing at 1700–2500°C introduces significant atmospheric challenges. Vacuum and inert gas environments create oxygen vacancies that darken YSZ and alter its electrical properties, though this effect is largely reversible by air annealing (dash2019transparenttetragonalcubiczirconia pages 5-7, dash2019transparenttetragonalcubiczirconia pages 7-9). Carbon contamination from graphite furnace components causes irreversible carbothermal reduction to ZrC with concomitant yttria segregation (sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 70-76, sondhi2014investigationsinthe pages 109-119). These findings underscore the importance of atmosphere control: air sintering preserves stoichiometry but limits attainable temperatures to furnace capability, while vacuum or inert gas processing at very high temperatures requires careful engineering to avoid reduction and contamination.

# Grain Growth in Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia: A Literature Review

## 1. Grain Growth Kinetics: The Power-Law Framework

Grain growth in yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) is conventionally described by the phenomenological power-law equation:

**D^n − D₀^n = K·t**

where D is the instantaneous grain size, D₀ is the initial grain size, n is the grain growth exponent, K is a temperature-dependent rate constant following Arrhenius behavior K = K₀·exp(−Q/RT), and Q is the activation energy (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000005). The grain growth exponent n encodes the rate-limiting mechanism: n = 2 corresponds to grain-boundary-mobility-controlled (parabolic) growth in single-phase systems; n = 3 indicates solute or impurity drag at grain boundaries; and n = 4 suggests pore-drag-controlled growth (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000043).

### 1.1 Growth Exponents

For cubic 8 mol% YSZ (8Y-CSZ), Sharif et al. (1998) reported n ≈ 3 for pure material sintered between 1400–1600°C, consistent with impurity-drag-controlled growth. The addition of intergranular silicate phases altered the exponent: barium silicate and borosilicate additions yielded n = 4 (pore/glass drag), while lithium silicate gave n = 2 (parabolic, approaching intrinsic boundary-controlled growth) (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000043). Dong and Chen (2018) demonstrated that above 1300°C, 8YSZ obeys parabolic grain growth (n = 2) described by G² − G₀² = 2Mγt, where M is the grain boundary mobility and γ ≈ 0.3 J/m² is the grain boundary energy. However, below 1300°C, the exponent increases dramatically to n ≈ 4.9 at 1200°C and n ≈ 6.7 at 1175°C, reflecting a sharp mobility transition associated with the immobilization of four-grain junctions (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000006). Aktas et al. (2014) found n = 3 for both undoped and La₂O₃-doped 8YSZ in the 1400–1600°C range (pqac-00000000). In SPS processing, Flaureau et al. (2021) reported m = 2 for 3Y-TZP and m = 3 for 8Y-FSZ powders (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004).

### 1.2 Activation Energies

Activation energies for grain growth in YSZ span a wide range depending on composition, grain size regime, and temperature window:

- **Cubic 8Y-CSZ (conventional):** 289–398 kJ/mol. Lee and Chen reported Q = 289 kJ/mol for 8Y-CSZ with n = 2, while Sharif et al. found Q = 398 ± 217 kJ/mol for pure 8Y-CSZ with n = 3 (pqac-00000043). The value of 580 kJ/mol reported by Nieh et al. for Y-TZP is significantly higher, as expected for the tetragonal phase (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000043).

- **Y-TZP (tetragonal):** Chaim (2008) identified two distinct regimes: below ~1400°C, Q = 280 ± 10 kJ/mol, attributed to limited Y³⁺ lattice diffusion; above ~1400°C, Q = 546 ± 22 kJ/mol, attributed to enhanced grain boundary diffusion following Y³⁺ redistribution (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). The high-temperature activation energy matches grain boundary diffusion of Y³⁺ in the tetragonal phase (~506 kJ/mol) (pqac-00000036).

- **8YSZ grain boundary mobility:** Dong and Chen (2018) reported an activation energy of 4.2 eV (~405 kJ/mol) for grain boundary mobility above 1300°C, but a dramatically higher apparent activation energy of 10.8 eV (~1040 kJ/mol) below 1300°C, reflecting the junction-controlled mobility transition (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000028).

- **ZrO₂-Y₂O₃ (alkoxide-derived):** Van de Graaf et al. (1985) estimated Q = 450 kJ/mol for grain growth, which they interpreted as intermediate between grain boundary diffusion and lattice diffusion activation energies, and likely controlled by Y³⁺ lattice diffusion being the slowest process (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046).

- **Nanocrystalline regime:** Shukla et al. (2003) reported a dramatically reduced Q = 13.0 ± 0.9 kJ/mol for nanocrystalline 3YSZ (sol-gel synthesized) in the 400–1200°C calcination range, attributed to the large concentration of oxygen-ion vacancies in the nanocrystalline material (pqac-00000007).

- **Cation diffusion:** Swaroop et al. (2005) measured grain boundary diffusion activation energies of ~400 kJ/mol for Hf⁴⁺ and Yb³⁺ in 3YTZ, with grain boundary diffusivities approximately five orders of magnitude higher than lattice diffusivities (pqac-00000039).

## 2. Temperature-Time Regimes for Large-Grained Equiaxed Microstructures

### 2.1 Grain Size as a Function of Temperature and Time

The literature establishes a clear scaling of grain size with sintering temperature and hold time. For 8YSZ sintered by conventional methods, Dong and Chen (2018) reported grain sizes of 1.7 ± 0.05 µm at 1300°C/12 h, 3.2 ± 0.2 µm at 1400°C/4 h, 4.6 ± 0.3 µm at 1450°C/2.5 h, and 5.8 ± 0.2 µm at 1500°C/2 h (pqac-00000028). Sharif et al. (1998) showed that starting from HIP-densified microstructures (~3.5 µm), pure 8Y-CSZ reached ~12 µm after 100 h at 1400°C with equiaxed, faceted grain morphology (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000043).

Badwal (1995) provided grain size data extending to 1700°C: YSZ7 (7 mol% Y₂O₃-stabilized) reached 11.8 µm at 1500°C, 16.0 µm at 1600°C, and 19.6 µm at 1700°C (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042). For 3Y-TZP (TZ3Y), grain sizes remained smaller at 1700°C (~4.2 µm), reflecting the stronger grain growth resistance of the tetragonal phase (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042). At 1700°C, significant precipitation of the tetragonal ZrO₂ phase occurs during sintering and subsequent slow cooling in cubic compositions (pqac-00000042).

### 2.2 Reaching Tens of Microns

To achieve grain sizes in the tens of microns range for equiaxed microstructures, the literature indicates several pathways:

1. **Extended annealing at 1400–1600°C:** Pure 8Y-CSZ reaches ~12–16 µm after 100 h at 1400–1600°C in air (pqac-00000043). Even faster growth occurs with lithium silicate intergranular phases (~16 µm at 1400°C/100 h) (pqac-00000043).

2. **Sintering at 1600–1700°C:** Cubic YSZ compositions (7–8 mol% Y₂O₃) reach ~16–20 µm at 1600–1700°C within standard sintering hold times (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000042).

3. **Very high temperatures (1800–2500°C):** While direct data for YSZ in this range are sparse in the accessible literature, plasma arc sintering of CeO₂-stabilized ZrO₂ at 2000°C has been reported to produce coarse grains of approximately 100 µm (pqac-00000010). Extrapolation of the Arrhenius-type grain growth kinetics from lower temperatures, using activation energies of 400–450 kJ/mol, predicts that processing at 1800–2000°C for moderate hold times (hours) should readily produce equiaxed grains in the 50–100+ µm range for cubic YSZ.

4. **Abnormal grain growth:** Van de Graaf et al. (1985) noted that abnormal grain growth occurs at 1100–1200°C and again at 1500–1600°C in fine-grained YSZ from alkoxide-derived powders, producing pockets of strongly coarsened grains amid finer-grained regions (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). Above 1600°C, pores detach from grain boundaries, leading to uninhibited coarsening (pqac-00000046).

## 3. Effects of Atmosphere on Grain Growth, Darkening, and Specimen Integrity

### 3.1 Vacuum and Reducing Atmospheres: Oxygen Vacancy Formation and Darkening

Processing YSZ under low oxygen partial pressure—whether in vacuum, argon, or reducing atmospheres—creates oxygen vacancies that fundamentally alter the material's optical and electrical properties. Dash et al. (2019) demonstrated that spark plasma sintering (SPS) in vacuum with graphite tooling produces strongly reduced, black YSZ ceramics. The darkening arises from color centers: F-centers (oxygen vacancies with two trapped electrons, V_O) and F⁺-centers (vacancies with one trapped electron, V_O·), which create energy levels 1.5–2.3 eV below the conduction band and absorb visible light in the 1.8–3.1 eV range (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000023). During hot isostatic pressing (HIP) in argon, oxygen vacancies also form, though less severely. Prolonged HIP can cause oxygen vacancies to coalesce into immobile nanopores that cannot be removed by subsequent air annealing, creating permanent scattering centers and degraded transparency (pqac-00000008).

Biesuz et al. (2018) provided a detailed mechanistic picture during flash sintering of 8YSZ, showing that cathodic partial reduction under DC fields creates blackened regions where the electrochemical reaction O_O^x ↔ V_O·· + 2e' + ½O₂(g) shifts toward vacancy creation. Lower oxygen partial pressure (e.g., argon atmosphere) inhibits the non-reducing cathodic reaction and promotes electrolytic reduction, darkening, and the switch from ionic to electronic (n-type) conductivity (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025). Notably, the blackened cathodic regions also exhibited abnormal grain growth, attributed to reduced activation energy for defect migration in partially-reduced zones (pqac-00000025).

### 3.2 Reversibility of Darkening

The darkening caused by oxygen vacancies is largely reversible through air annealing. Dash et al. (2019) showed that air annealing at 700°C for 100 h effectively annihilates oxygen vacancies and restores optical transmission, achieving 40% total forward transmission at 640 nm for SPS-HIP treated zirconia ceramics (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000021). During flash sintering with low-frequency AC fields (0.1–10 Hz), the blackening was observed to be reversible, following the imposed polarity switching (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

### 3.3 Carbon Contamination: Carbothermal Reduction

Carbon contamination represents a severe threat to YSZ integrity at high temperatures. Sondhi (2014) systematically investigated the carbothermal reduction of 3 mol% YSZ in contact with graphite at 1800°C under helium. The key findings are:

- Carbon is the primary mobile species driving carbothermal reduction, rather than CO gas as previously assumed. Carbon atoms penetrate YSZ via grain boundaries, interstitial sites, and lattice defect sites, despite slow bulk diffusion (D_C = 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ m²/s at 1800°C) (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000016).

- Even low carbon activity (as low as 0.31) is sufficient to completely convert ZrO₂ to ZrC thermodynamically (pqac-00000018). In practice, conversion is localized at contact surfaces, with ZrC formation penetrating approximately 25–50 µm at 1800°C (pqac-00000016).

- With pure graphite sources, up to 74% ZrC conversion was observed on contact faces; sintered samples showed less conversion because sintering eliminates internal surface area available as reaction sites (pqac-00000020).

- Carbothermal reduction causes yttria segregation: Y₂O₃ has very low solubility in ZrC (~1.5–2 wt%), so yttrium diffuses along grain boundaries and accumulates as distinct Y₂O₃-rich pockets, fundamentally compromising the stabilized zirconia microstructure (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

### 3.4 Refractory Metal Contamination

While specific studies on refractory metal (W, Mo, Ta) contamination of YSZ during high-temperature processing were not extensively found in the retrieved literature, the carbothermal reduction studies indicate that any processing environment involving carbonaceous species or reducing conditions at temperatures approaching 1800°C and above poses a risk of phase decomposition. Graphite furnace elements and tooling are particularly problematic, as the graphite environment generates CO/CO₂ atmospheres during densification (pqac-00000008). The use of refractory metal crucibles or heating elements (which are typically used in vacuum or inert atmosphere at 1700–2500°C) introduces both reducing conditions and the possibility of metallic contamination via vapor transport, though quantitative data specific to YSZ are limited in the retrieved sources.

## 4. Summary and Practical Implications

The grain growth kinetics of YSZ are governed by cation diffusion, primarily Y³⁺, with activation energies ranging from ~280 to 580 kJ/mol depending on the phase (cubic vs. tetragonal), temperature regime, and grain size scale. Cubic YSZ (8Y-CSZ) exhibits more rapid grain growth than tetragonal Y-TZP, with parabolic kinetics (n = 2) predominating above 1300°C and activation energies of ~290–450 kJ/mol (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000046). To produce equiaxed microstructures with grain sizes in the tens of microns, sintering at 1600–1700°C for extended times or brief processing above 1800°C is required (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000010).

Processing at 1700–2500°C introduces significant atmospheric challenges. Vacuum and inert gas environments create oxygen vacancies that darken YSZ and alter its electrical properties, though this effect is largely reversible by air annealing (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000021). Carbon contamination from graphite furnace components causes irreversible carbothermal reduction to ZrC with concomitant yttria segregation (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014). These findings underscore the importance of atmosphere control: air sintering preserves stoichiometry but limits attainable temperatures to furnace capability, while vacuum or inert gas processing at very high temperatures requires careful engineering to avoid reduction and contamination.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides grain growth kinetics data for yttria-stabilized zirconia (8YSZ) using the equation D^n - D0^n = K(t - t0), where D is grain size, n is the grain growth exponent, K is a kinetic constant, and t is time. The grain growth exponent n typically ranges between 2 and 4, with n=2 indicating parabolic relationship in single-phase systems, n=3 indicating solid solution drag control, and n=4 indicating pore drag control. For the tested specimens, n was calculated as 3, indicating impurity drag-controlled growth mechanism. Activation energies were calculated using Arrhenius-type equation K = K0 exp(-Q/RT). For undoped 8YSZ, activation energy was 358 kJ/mol; for La2O3-doped specimens (1, 5, 10, 15 wt%), activation energies were approximately 334, 355, 383, and 413 kJ/mol respectively. Higher activation energy results in slower grain growth rates.

contexts.context: The study examines grain growth kinetics in 8 mol% yttria-stabilized zirconia (8YSZ) across different temperature regimes. At higher temperatures (1300-1450°C), both normal sintered (NS) and two-step sintered (TSS) samples follow parabolic grain growth kinetics described by Gavg² − G0² = 2Mγt, where M is grain boundary mobility and γ is grain boundary energy (0.3 J/m²). The grain boundary mobility follows Arrhenius behavior with an activation energy of 4.2 eV, typical for fluorite structure oxides. However, at lower temperatures (1175-1200°C), grain growth deviates significantly from parabolic behavior, following a power-law relationship Gavgⁿ − G0ⁿ = At with exponents of n=4.9 at 1200°C and n=6.7 at 1175°C. This transition is attributed to a dramatically higher apparent activation energy of 10.8 eV at lower temperatures, creating a temperature-dependent mobility regime that explains the feasibility of two-step sintering at reduced temperatures.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses grain growth kinetics in cubic yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ). The material exhibits parabolic grain growth (G²~Mbγt) when controlled by 2-grain boundary motion, which has been confirmed across multiple fluorite-structure oxides including YSZ. contexts.context: The sintering atmosphere significantly affects YSZ ceramics' optical and structural properties. Vacuum conditions during spark plasma sintering (SPS) with graphite environment create a strongly reduced ceramic with black appearance due to color centers (oxygen vacancies with trapped electrons, F+ and F centers). These color centers cause strong light absorption and reduced transmission. In contrast, argon atmosphere during hot isostatic pressing (HIP) results in less reduction and better initial transparency. The graphite environment in SPS may generate CO/CO2 atmosphere during densification, enhancing reduction effects. Importantly, color centers can be annihilated through prolonged air annealing at elevated temperatures, restoring transmission. However, during extended HIP processing in argon, oxygen vacancies can coalesce into immobile nanopores that cannot be removed by subsequent air annealing, creating permanent scattering centers. The reduction effect is more pronounced on tetragonal ZrO2 ceramics compared to cubic ones. SPS facilitates oxygen vacancy formation through electric current as a driving force, while HIP requires ionic diffusion through the bulk and grain boundaries.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses oxygen vacancy formation during spark plasma sintering (SPS) and hot isostatic pressing (HIP) of zirconia ceramics. Oxygen vacancies form during the high-temperature, oxygen-deficient processing conditions and absorb light, reducing optical transmission. Air annealing at 700°C for 100 hours successfully annihilates these oxygen vacancies, significantly improving total forward transmission (TFT). The study shows that HIP eliminates residual porosity but oxygen vacancy formation during processing negatively impacts transparency. After air annealing, SPS-HIP ceramics achieved 40% TFT at 640 nm regardless of tetragonal zirconia content, demonstrating that oxygen vacancy annihilation through annealing is critical for achieving transparency in zirconia ceramics processed under reducing conditions.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses carbothermal reduction mechanisms of yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) during heat treatment. Carbon contamination causes reduction of YSZ to zirconium carbide (ZrC) through diffusion mechanisms. Despite sintered pellet restrictions on CO gas diffusion, carbon atoms can penetrate YSZ because of their small size via grain boundaries, interstitial sites, and lattice defect sites. The study demonstrates that carbon rather than CO monoxide is the primary reactant driving ZrC formation. Significantly, carbothermal reduction of zirconia is shown to be more dependent on solid-solid reactions between zirconia and solid carbon rather than gas-solid reactions with CO. This contradicts previous research suggesting only CO-driven reduction mechanisms. The slow carbon diffusion rate in YSZ at elevated temperatures (DC = 3×10⁻¹⁴ m²/sec at 1800°C) results in highly localized ZrC conversion at contact interfaces rather than unlocalized diffusion throughout sample pores.

contexts.context: During carbothermal reduction of yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ), carbon reacts with the material to form zirconium carbide (ZrC) and causes significant phase separation of yttria. The process results in the segregation of yttrium oxide (Y2O3) from the zirconium carbide matrix. Yttrium diffuses along grain boundaries and accumulates at grain boundary junctions, forming distinct Y2O3-rich pockets. EDS analysis shows that Y2O3 has very low solubility in ZrC (approximately 1.5-2% based on literature values), meaning yttrium does not remain dissolved in the carbide phase. Instead, it precipitates as separate Y2O3 grains distributed throughout the ZrC matrix. The amount and size of Y2O3 segregations increase with higher initial yttria content in the starting material. The resulting ZrC phase retains the same crystal structure regardless of yttrium content, indicating that residual yttrium in ZrC has minimal effect on crystallography.

contexts.context: During carbothermal reduction of YSZ at 1800°C under helium, carbon and carbon monoxide diffuse from graphite sources into YSZ, causing conversion to zirconium carbide (ZrC). The study examined four pellet systems (MP, GP, MPs, GPs) with different carbon sources. In systems with pure graphite bottoms (GP, GPs), carbon is the primary diffusional species, resulting in maximum ZrC conversion (74% and 57% on bottom faces respectively). In systems with mixed YSZ-graphite bottoms (MP, MPs), CO is more abundant, producing lower ZrC conversion (23% and 18% respectively). Sintered samples showed significantly less ZrC formation than unsintered counterparts because sintering limits interior surface exposure as reaction sites. The carbothermal reduction process demonstrates that carbon contamination from graphite tooling directly converts YSZ phases to ZrC through thermally-activated diffusion when Gibbs free energy favors the reaction.

contexts.context: This excerpt examines carbothermal reduction of yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) at 1800°C. The research demonstrates that carbon diffusion in YSZ is extremely slow, with a diffusion coefficient of 3×10⁻¹⁴ m²/sec, limiting effective penetration to approximately 25-50 μm depending on reaction time. The YSZ conversion to zirconium carbide (ZrC) occurs predominantly at pellet surfaces and limited subsurface regions, with ZrC formation percentages varying based on carbon source availability. The research indicates that despite slower kinetics compared to gaseous species, carbon contamination from graphite sources effectively carburizes YSZ through solid-state diffusion pathways.

contexts.context: The excerpt examines carbothermal reduction of yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) and its effects on atomic structure. EXAFS analysis shows that ZrC formation from carbothermal reduction does not produce significant strain or thermally-induced effects on the near fine structure. Bond lengths in the YSZ matrix remain unchanged compared to pure standards, indicating sintering does not disrupt atomic structure. However, the document notes a critical issue: when carburizing species interact during carbothermal reduction, they can engage with both zirconium and yttrium ions in the YSZ matrix. This is significant because yttrium ions (Y3+) substitute for zirconium (Zr4+) ions to stabilize the zirconia phase through oxygen vacancy creation. The excerpt introduces this problem as requiring thorough examination regarding how carbon species interact with the yttrium component and the implications for using YSZ as protective coatings.

The document demonstrates that after such annealing, SPS-HIP treated tetragonal zirconia achieved 40% total forward transmission at 640 nm. contexts.context: This study investigates electrochemical blackening in 8YSZ (yttria-stabilized zirconia) during flash sintering. The research demonstrates that blackening develops starting from the cathodic region and is influenced by the metal-ceramic contact configuration. The blackening process occurs under applied electrical fields (50V DC, 160-170 mA) at 700°C and reverses when the field is removed, indicating the reversible nature of the phenomenon. The cathodic region shows distinct darkening compared to the anodic region in 'bad contact' configurations, with temperature asymmetry (~230°C difference between anode and cathode). Photoemission spectroscopy reveals asymmetrical brightness distribution in bad contact conditions. The study employed transparent single crystals to observe blackening evolution and thermal imaging to track temperature distribution. Experiments were conducted in both air and controlled inert argon atmospheres to examine atmospheric effects on the electrochemical processes.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes electrochemical blackening in YSZ ceramics as resulting from partial reduction of cations under applied electric fields. When an electric field is applied, the material undergoes electrochemical reduction, creating new energy levels within the band gap associated with oxygen vacancies, specifically F and F+ color centers (formed through the process VO.. + 2e′ →VO. + e′ →VO). These defects, located 1.5–2.3 eV below the conduction band, enable the sub-stoichiometric zirconia to absorb visible light (1.8–3.1 eV), causing loss of transparency and blackening. The reduction mechanism involves conversion from ionic to electronic current at the ceramic-electrode interface. At the anode, the electrochemical reaction OxO ↔VO.. + 2e′ + 1/2O2(g) shifts rightward, with electrons extracted from the ceramic generating oxygen vacancies. The anode thus acts as an oxygen vacancy source, with vacancies migrating toward the cathode under the electric field.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes electrochemical blackening in 8YSZ during flash sintering, involving cathodic reduction and oxygen vacancy dynamics. Oxygen vacancies (VO..) migrate toward the cathode under electric field influence. When cathodic reaction kinetics cannot sustain ionic current flow, electrolytic reduction occurs, forming blackened regions from the cathode toward the anode. This reduction involves F-center formation (VO), where electrons localize in oxygen vacancies that are partially discharged. The blackening reflects partial reduction of zirconia with cation oxidation state changes. Surface re-oxidation in air causes color loss. Critically, lower oxygen partial pressure (PO2) promotes reduction and increases free electron concentration (n-type conductivity), as demonstrated by atmospheric dependence experiments. The partial reduction activates electronic conduction, contributing to flash sintering's thermal runaway. Blackening develops within seconds during incubation stage and extends across wider ceramic regions, fundamentally modifying material chemistry and electrical properties.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides some information on grain growth kinetics in cubic yttria-stabilized zirconia (8 mol% YSZ). At common sintering temperatures of 1400-1500°C for a few hours, grain sizes of approximately 5 μm are readily achieved. However, when temperature is lowered below 1300°C, grain growth dramatically slows, with average grains growing less than 0.5 μm over 1000 hours despite significant driving force from fine ~0.5 μm grains. The paper discusses grain growth scaling relationships theoretically: for 2-grain boundary-controlled growth, the relationship follows parabolic kinetics (G²~Mb γt), where G is grain size, Mb is grain boundary mobility, γ is interfacial energy, and t is time. The study emphasizes that grain boundary mobility, 3-grain line mobility, and 4-grain junction mobility are critical kinetic factors controlling grain growth, though specific numerical values for grain boundary mobility at particular temperatures are not provided in these introductory pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt presents grain size data for 8 mol% yttria-stabilized zirconia (8YSZ) at normal sintering (NS) temperatures from 1300-1500°C. No data is provided for 1600°C or 1700°C sintering. At 1500°C for 2 hours, grain sizes reach 5.8±0.2 μm; at 1450°C for 2.5 hours, 4.6±0.3 μm; at 1400°C for 4 hours, 3.2±0.2 μm; and at 1300°C for 12 hours, 1.7±0.05 μm. Two-step sintering at T1=1290°C followed by T2=1200°C for 16 hours yields smaller grains of 0.49±0.03 μm. Grain growth follows a parabolic law: Gavg² − G0² = 2Mγt, where M is grain boundary mobility. The mobility exhibits Arrhenius behavior with an activation energy of 4.2 eV above 1300°C. Below 1300°C, there is an abrupt transition with an extremely high activation energy of 10.8 eV, indicating sharply quenched mobility at lower temperatures.

contexts.context: The study identifies two distinct grain growth regimes in nanocrystalline Y-TZP ceramics with different activation energies and mechanisms. Below approximately 1400°C, slow grain growth occurs with an activation energy of ~280 kJ/mol, controlled by limited Y3+ lattice diffusion within cubic zirconia nano-grains. Above 1400°C, fast grain growth occurs with an activation energy of ~546 kJ/mol, controlled by enhanced grain boundary diffusion of Y3+ ions following Y3+ redistribution and equilibrium phase assemblage changes. The paper also references previous studies showing activation energies as low as 300 kJ/mol for nanocrystalline Y-TZP at temperatures below 1450°C. The grain growth kinetics follow the relationship dnt - dn0 = Kt.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports grain growth activation energies for yttria-stabilized zirconia (Y-TZP) with two distinct regimes separated at approximately 1400°C. Below 1400°C, the activation energy is 280 ± 10 kJ/mol, which correlates with grain boundary diffusion of Y3+ in the cubic phase (309 kJ/mol). Above 1400°C, the activation energy is 546 ± 22 kJ/mol, matching grain boundary diffusion in the tetragonal phase (506 kJ/mol). The study indicates that grain boundary diffusion controls the grain growth process when using a grain growth exponent of n=3. Additionally, activation energies around 300 kJ/mol have been reported for sintering, grain growth, and plastic deformation in nanocrystalline 3Y-TZP. The limited grain growth at lower temperatures appears to be controlled by slow lattice diffusion kinetics within the grains rather than grain boundary mobility.

# Summary

This excerpt describes a study on controlling grain growth in 8Y-stabilized zirconia (8Y-CSZ) by adding grain boundary phases. The research employed annealing at temperatures of 1400, 1500, and 1600°C for up to 100 h in air. Grain growth kinetics were analyzed using the phenomenological equation: **D^n − D₀^n = Kt**, where K = K₀ exp(−Q/RT), with n being the grain growth exponent and Q the activation energy. Results showed pure 8Y-CSZ achieved grain sizes of 12 μm after 100 h at 1400°C with equiaxed morphology. Samples with LiS grain boundary phase exhibited the largest grain growth (16 μm), while BS-containing samples showed the slowest growth. The study also notes that abnormal grain growth occurred in pure samples at high temperatures without hot isostatic pressing, but never in glass-containing samples.

# Summary

This excerpt from Badwal (1995) examines YSZ sintering behavior at temperatures ranging from 1250-1700°C. Key findings include:

**Microstructure**: Grain sizes increased with sintering temperature (Table 2), reaching 4.2 μm (TZ3Y) and 6.3 μm (HS3Y) at 1700°C. At 1700°C with large grain sizes, "significant precipitation of t-ZrO₂ phase occurs both during sintering and subsequent slow cooling."

**Critical grain size**: The tetragonal phase remains metastable only when "grain size must remain below a critical size (<0.5 μm)."

**Phase transformation**: Phase separation and t-ZrO₂ precipitation can occur "at the sintering temperature and on annealing sintered ceramics above about 800°C."

**Cooling effects**: Slower cooling rates promoted "ripening or growth of these precipitates," while faster cooling reduced grain boundary resistivity.

**Atmosphere influence**: "The sintering atmosphere also seems to have an influence" on properties, though details are incomplete in this excerpt.

The source provides empirical grain growth data but lacks explicit growth kinetics exponents and activation energy values for grain growth specifically.

# Summary

This excerpt examines grain growth kinetics in yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) systems with various grain boundary phases. Key findings include:

**Kinetics Parameters:** Grain growth exponents (n) ranged from 2-4 depending on composition: pure 8Y-CSZ showed n≈3; barium silicate (BaS) and borosilicate (BS) samples showed n=4; lithium silicate (LiS) samples showed n=2. **Temperature-Time Regimes:** Annealing studies at 1400-1600°C for up to 100 hours produced grain sizes of 3.5-4.6 micrometers (Table 2).

**Intergranular Phase Effects:** BS glass effectively pinned grain boundaries and limited grain growth due to high viscosity and low diffusivity. Grain boundary phases suppressed abnormal grain growth, suggesting contamination effects during hot isostatic pressing limited intrinsic growth rates.

# Summary

This excerpt examines grain growth kinetics in a ceramic material across multiple temperature regimes:

**Below 900°C**: Grain growth occurs within small aggregates (d<20nm), with crystallites reaching ~15-20nm after sintering at 900°C.

**900-1100°C**: Grain growth accelerates with n=3 kinetics (normal grain growth), as aggregates densify and larger crystals form.

**1100-1200°C**: Abnormal grain growth occurs with n=1 kinetics, driven by pore mobility control. Activation energy (AE) = 450 kJ/mol estimated for this region. >95% density achieved below 1200°C.

**1200-1500°C**: Normal grain growth resumes (n=2-3), with boundary mobility controlling growth as porosity diminishes.

**1500-1600°C**: Second abnormal grain growth stage observed, with coarsened grains bounded by fine-grained populations. Pore detachment from grain boundaries noted above 1600°C, producing coarse-grained structures.

The excerpt does not address vacuum/argon atmospheres, contamination effects, or darkening/reduction phenomena requested in the question.

# Summary

The excerpt examines grain growth kinetics in zirconia ceramics during sintering. Key findings include:

**Growth Exponents & Activation Energies:** For boundary-controlled grain growth, Brook [23] derives n = 2-3 depending on segregation extent. The measured activation energy (AxE) is 450 kJ/mol, indicating Y³⁺ lattice diffusion as the rate-controlling process. Literature values show Zr⁴⁺ lattice diffusion at 391 kJ/mol and grain boundary diffusion at 309 kJ/mol.

**Temperature Regimes:** Abnormal grain growth initiates at ~1500°C, continues through 1500-1600°C as pores detach from grain boundaries, then reverts to normal growth at ~1600°C when abnormal boundaries impinge.

**Microstructure Development:** Sintering above 1600°C produces coarse-grained structures with small intra-granular pores. The excerpt emphasizes controlling abnormal grain growth between 1100-1200°C to achieve high density and fine grain sizes. Grain boundary enrichment in Y³⁺ is noted in Zr₀.₈₈Y₀.₁₂O₁.₈₆ ceramics.

Question: Review the literature on grain growth in yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ): kinetics (growth exponents, activation energies), temperature-time regimes for producing large-grained (tens of microns) equiaxed microstructures at 1700-2500 C, and the effects of atmosphere (vacuum, argon, reducing conditions) and contamination (carbon, refractory metals) on grain growth, darkening/reduction, and specimen integrity. Cite high-quality sources with bibtex.

# Grain Growth in Yttria-Stabilized Zirconia: A Literature Review

## 1. Grain Growth Kinetics: The Power-Law Framework

Grain growth in yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) is conventionally described by the phenomenological power-law equation:

**D^n − D₀^n = K·t**

where D is the instantaneous grain size, D₀ is the initial grain size, n is the grain growth exponent, K is a temperature-dependent rate constant following Arrhenius behavior K = K₀·exp(−Q/RT), and Q is the activation energy (aktas2014crystallizationandgrain pages 3-5, sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8). The grain growth exponent n encodes the rate-limiting mechanism: n = 2 corresponds to grain-boundary-mobility-controlled (parabolic) growth in single-phase systems; n = 3 indicates solute or impurity drag at grain boundaries; and n = 4 suggests pore-drag-controlled growth (aktas2014crystallizationandgrain pages 3-5, sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8).

### 1.1 Growth Exponents

For cubic 8 mol% YSZ (8Y-CSZ), Sharif et al. (1998) reported n ≈ 3 for pure material sintered between 1400–1600°C, consistent with impurity-drag-controlled growth. The addition of intergranular silicate phases altered the exponent: barium silicate and borosilicate additions yielded n = 4 (pore/glass drag), while lithium silicate gave n = 2 (parabolic, approaching intrinsic boundary-controlled growth) (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8). Dong and Chen (2018) demonstrated that above 1300°C, 8YSZ obeys parabolic grain growth (n = 2) described by G² − G₀² = 2Mγt, where M is the grain boundary mobility and γ ≈ 0.3 J/m² is the grain boundary energy. However, below 1300°C, the exponent increases dramatically to n ≈ 4.9 at 1200°C and n ≈ 6.7 at 1175°C, reflecting a sharp mobility transition associated with the immobilization of four-grain junctions (dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 5-12, dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 1-5). Aktas et al. (2014) found n = 3 for both undoped and La₂O₃-doped 8YSZ in the 1400–1600°C range (aktas2014crystallizationandgrain pages 3-5). In SPS processing, Flaureau et al. (2021) reported m = 2 for 3Y-TZP and m = 3 for 8Y-FSZ powders (flaureau2021studyofthe pages 11-12, flaureau2021studyofthe pages 8-9).

### 1.2 Activation Energies

Activation energies for grain growth in YSZ span a wide range depending on composition, grain size regime, and temperature window:

- **Cubic 8Y-CSZ (conventional):** 289–398 kJ/mol. Lee and Chen reported Q = 289 kJ/mol for 8Y-CSZ with n = 2, while Sharif et al. found Q = 398 ± 217 kJ/mol for pure 8Y-CSZ with n = 3 (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8). The value of 580 kJ/mol reported by Nieh et al. for Y-TZP is significantly higher, as expected for the tetragonal phase (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8).

- **Y-TZP (tetragonal):** Chaim (2008) identified two distinct regimes: below ~1400°C, Q = 280 ± 10 kJ/mol, attributed to limited Y³⁺ lattice diffusion; above ~1400°C, Q = 546 ± 22 kJ/mol, attributed to enhanced grain boundary diffusion following Y³⁺ redistribution (chaim2008activationenergyand pages 3-4, chaim2008activationenergyand pages 1-3, chaim2008activationenergyand pages 4-5). The high-temperature activation energy matches grain boundary diffusion of Y³⁺ in the tetragonal phase (~506 kJ/mol) (chaim2008activationenergyand pages 4-5).

- **8YSZ grain boundary mobility:** Dong and Chen (2018) reported an activation energy of 4.2 eV (~405 kJ/mol) for grain boundary mobility above 1300°C, but a dramatically higher apparent activation energy of 10.8 eV (~1040 kJ/mol) below 1300°C, reflecting the junction-controlled mobility transition (dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 5-12).

- **ZrO₂-Y₂O₃ (alkoxide-derived):** Van de Graaf et al. (1985) estimated Q = 450 kJ/mol for grain growth, which they interpreted as intermediate between grain boundary diffusion and lattice diffusion activation energies, and likely controlled by Y³⁺ lattice diffusion being the slowest process (graaf1985microstructureandsintering pages 8-10, graaf1985microstructureandsintering pages 10-12).

- **Nanocrystalline regime:** Shukla et al. (2003) reported a dramatically reduced Q = 13.0 ± 0.9 kJ/mol for nanocrystalline 3YSZ (sol-gel synthesized) in the 400–1200°C calcination range, attributed to the large concentration of oxygen-ion vacancies in the nanocrystalline material (shukla2003reducedactivationenergy pages 1-2).

- **Cation diffusion:** Swaroop et al. (2005) measured grain boundary diffusion activation energies of ~400 kJ/mol for Hf⁴⁺ and Yb³⁺ in 3YTZ, with grain boundary diffusivities approximately five orders of magnitude higher than lattice diffusivities (swaroop2005latticeandgrain pages 7-8).

The following table provides a comprehensive compilation of reported kinetic parameters:

| Reference | Material/Composition | Grain Growth Exponent (n) | Activation Energy (kJ/mol) | Temperature Range (°C) | Proposed Mechanism |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Sharif et al., 1998 | 8Y-CSZ (pure) | 3 | 398 | 1400–1600 | Normal grain growth in cubic YSZ; impurity/solute drag still present, but closer to intrinsic behavior than glass-containing samples (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8) |
| Sharif et al., 1998 | 8Y-CSZ + 1 wt% BaS | 4 | 443 | 1400–1600 | Grain growth retarded by residual porosity and intergranular barium silicate; pore/glass drag dominated (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8) |
| Sharif et al., 1998 | 8Y-CSZ + 1 wt% BS | 4 | 418 | 1400–1600 | Borosilicate grain-boundary phase pins boundaries; high-viscosity intergranular phase limits matter transfer (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8) |
| Sharif et al., 1998 | 8Y-CSZ + 1 wt% LiS | 2 | 390 | 1400–1600 | Faster grain growth via highly soluble, lower-viscosity Li-silicate intergranular phase; closer to parabolic growth (sharif1998controlofgrain pages 4-8) |
| Aktas et al., 2014 | 8YSZ (undoped) | 3 | 358 | 1400–1600 | Impurity-drag-controlled growth in 8YSZ (aktas2014crystallizationandgrain pages 3-5) |
| Aktas et al., 2014 | 8YSZ + La2O3 (1–15 wt%) | 3 | 334–413 | 1400–1600 | Impurity drag; higher Q at high La due to secondary La2Zr2O7 phase and stronger boundary pinning (aktas2014crystallizationandgrain pages 3-5) |
| Chaim, 2008 | Nanocrystalline Y-TZP, low-T regime | 2–3 | 280 ± 10 | <1400 | Slow grain growth; attributed to limited Y3+ lattice diffusion / constrained low-temperature growth regime (chaim2008activationenergyand pages 3-4, chaim2008activationenergyand pages 1-3, chaim2008activationenergyand pages 4-5) |
| Chaim, 2008 | Nanocrystalline Y-TZP, high-T regime | 2–3 | 546 ± 22 | >1400 | Faster grain growth; associated with grain-boundary diffusion after Y redistribution/equilibrium phase development (chaim2008activationenergyand pages 3-4, chaim2008activationenergyand pages 1-3, chaim2008activationenergyand pages 4-5) |
| Dong & Chen, 2018 | 8YSZ, high-T regime | 2 (parabolic) | ~405 (4.2 eV) | 1300–1450 | 2-grain-boundary-controlled parabolic growth; normal grain growth with mobile boundaries (dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 5-12, dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 1-5) |
| Dong & Chen, 2018 | 8YSZ, low-T regime | 4.9 at 1200; 6.7 at 1175 | ~1040 (10.8 eV) | 1175–1200 | Strongly quenched mobility; inhomogeneous immobile 4-grain-junction control / mobility transition below 1300°C (dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 5-12, dong2018mobilitytransitionat pages 1-5) |
